newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Mosenergo 1996 GAAP profits leap 56 pct.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Mosenergo 1996 GAAP profits leap 56 pct.

text.p: Russia's biggest regional power company Mosenergo announced on Monday that its net profit had risen more than 50 percent in 1996, according to U.S. accounting standards.
But the company made it clear it was prepared to cut off supplies to customers who do not pay their bills -- a common problem in Russia -- even at the cost of lower output.

OAO Energetiki i Elektrifikatsii Mosenergo, which supplies electricity and heating to the Moscow region, saw net profit rise 56 percent to $598 million from $383 million according to U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP).
Earnings per share rose 44 percent to $0.23 per share from $0.16 in 1995, while sales rose 41 percent to $4.13 billion.
The figures, audited by international accountancy firm Arthur Andersen, were issued by Mosenergo's financial adviser Salomon Bros, which is preparing a Eurobond issue for Mosenergo.
Earlier Mosenergo, which accounts for 10 percent of the electricity produced in Russia, was awarded a BB- credit rating by Standard & Poor's, the same rating as the Russian Federation.

The figures showed a much larger jump in profits than those issued previously to Russian accounting standards, which reflected only supplies actually paid for, and showed a profit rise of 14 percent in 1996.

Since then Mosenergo, in which national power company Unified Energy System (UES) EESR.RTS owns a 49 percent stake, has issued figures for the first quarter of this year, showing profits and energy output both falling.
"We are prepared to lower our total output in order to tighten payment discipline amongst our customers," Chief Executive Nestor Serebryannikov said in a statement.

But while electricity production in the first quarter of this year was eight percent lower than a year ago, and heating output was down 10 percent, the collection rate for sales rose to 71.2 percent from 51.7 percent.

Russian energy companies are among the biggest victims, as well as the main offenders, in the web of unpaid bills choking the Russian economy. Customers do not pay for their power, and the companies do not pay their energy suppliers in turn.

Companies are also behind on their tax payments, forcing the government to get tough with tax debtors, threatening to declare the largest companies bankrupt unless they agree a schedule of payments of arrears secured by asset-backed bonds or shares.
Mosenergo closed on the Russian Trading System on Monday at $1.268 after $1.259 on Friday.
